publisher: Bahdanau et al. · Université de Montréal
title: A close read of Bahdanau attention: every word looks back, and attention begins here
summary: Seq2Seq compresses an entire sentence into a fixed-length vector, so long sentences lose information. Bahdanau et al. made the decoder look back at every source word before generating each target word—score them and take a weighted sum—and the attention mechanism was born. We compute one attention step by hand, unpack the bidirectional encoder and alignment maps, then trace the path to the Transformer.
ai_summary: “Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate” (Université de Montréal, 2014) argues that the encoder-decoder's fixed-length vector is the bottleneck. It uses a bidirectional RNN encoder to leave one annotation vector for each source word. Every time the decoder generates a word, a small network scores all of the annotations, turns those scores into softmax weights, and takes a weighted sum to produce a context vector for that step, training alignment and translation together. On WMT'14 English-to-French, RNNsearch-50 scored 26.75 BLEU versus 17.82 without attention; trained longer, it reached 28.45, and on sentences without unknown words it beat Moses 36.15 to 35.63. Long sentences no longer degraded, and the weights can be drawn as alignment maps.
brief: Problem: the encoder-decoder compresses the whole sentence into a fixed-length vector, and translation quality drops quickly as sentences get longer.
Method: a bidirectional RNN leaves one vector for each source word; at each step the decoder scores them, applies softmax, and takes a weighted sum to get a context vector specific to that step.

Result: BLEU rises from 17.82 to 26.75, long sentences no longer degrade; on sentences without unknown words it beats the statistical MT system Moses, and the weights can be plotted as alignment maps.

Limits: compute grows with the product of source and target length, rare words are handled poorly, and it is still a recurrent network that is hard to parallelize; the Transformer later carried the idea much further.

cover.headline: Bahdanau attention, close read
cover.highlight: Every translated word looks back at the source

sections.h: The bottom line: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In September 2014, Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, and Yoshua Bengio of the Université de Montréal released this paper, later published at ICLR 2015. It targets the weakness from our previous close read of Seq2Seq: **the encoder must squash the entire sentence into a fixed-length vector**.

The paper's approach: instead of handing over only the last vector, the encoder leaves one vector for **each word** in the source sentence. Each time the decoder generates a word, it looks back over those vectors, works out which words matter right now, and takes a weighted average according to how much attention each one deserves. That gives a context vector built specifically for this step. In the paper's own words, this “implements a mechanism of **attention** in the decoder.”

Long sentences show the clearest effect. Without attention, translation quality falls off a cliff as sentences get longer; with attention, even sentences over 50 words do not degrade. A single model's BLEU rose from 17.82 to 26.75, then to 28.45 with longer training. On sentences without unknown words, it even beat the traditional statistical translation system Moses, 36.15 to 35.63.

This was attention's first major success in machine translation. Three years later, the Transformer pushed the idea to its logical extreme, removing the recurrent network and keeping only attention. Today, every layer of every large language model does what this paper started: **when it is about to output something, it searches the input for the relevant parts**.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: Don't squash the whole sentence into a single vector; keep one vector per word instead. At each decoder step, use a small network to score those vectors, turn the scores into softmax weights, and take a weighted sum to get that step's context vector. The weights themselves are a “soft alignment” table showing which source words each translated word came from.

callout.title: Three small concepts you'll need
callout.text: If they are new to you, these three are enough:
list: **Encoder-decoder**: one recurrent network reads the source sentence into a vector, and another generates the translation from that vector. See the previous close read in this series, Seq2Seq.
**Softmax**: turns any set of scores into positive numbers that add up to 1, with higher scores receiving a larger share.
**Weighted average**: multiply each vector by a weight, then add the results. When the weights sum to 1, the result lands “between” those vectors, closer to the one with the largest weight.

sections.h: The problem: a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck

blocks.p: The paper opens by pointing out the potential problem with the encoder-decoder architecture: a neural network has to compress all the necessary information about a source sentence into a fixed-length vector. That is hard for long sentences, especially sentences longer than those in the training data. Cho et al., from the same group, had already observed that basic encoder-decoder translation quality **deteriorates rapidly** as input sentences get longer.

plain.title: Cramming a whole sentence into a small box
plain.text: The original encoder has to squeeze an entire sentence, however long, into the same fixed-size vector c (the small red box). When the sentence is long, the box cannot hold everything, details are lost, and translation quality drops sharply.

callout.title: Like a translator allowed a single sticky note
callout.text: Imagine a translator who listens to a whole passage but is allowed to write only key points on one sticky note, then must translate from that note without looking at the original. Short sentences are fine. When the sentence is long, the note runs out of room, and details from the second half are lost or guessed. Attention is like letting that translator glance back at the source while writing, checking whichever part is needed.

blocks.p: Seq2Seq eased training by reversing the source sentence and reported that long sentences did not collapse. But that model used an 8000-dimensional sentence vector and a 4-layer LSTM. This paper targets the structural bottleneck itself: **no matter how long the sentence is, the representation is always the same size**.

sections.h: Core idea: for every generated word, soft-search the source sentence again

blocks.p: The paper calls the new model **RNNsearch** (an RNN that searches), with attention-free RNNencdec as the control. The most important difference from the basic encoder-decoder is that it does **not** try to encode the whole sentence into a fixed-length vector. Instead, it encodes the sentence into a sequence of vectors and adaptively selects some of them while decoding.
In the original encoder-decoder, every generated word uses the same sentence vector c. In the new model, generating the i-th word uses a **context vector computed specifically for it**, c_i:

parts.desc: y_i: the i-th target word to be generated
s_i: the decoder's hidden state at step i, roughly where the translation is and what should come next
c_i: the context vector specific to step i. The old model shares one c across all steps; this is the key difference.
Two nonlinear functions: g outputs the probability of the next word, and f updates the decoder state.

blocks.p: How is c_i computed? Three steps: **score, normalize, take a weighted sum**.

formula.expr:
e_{ij} = a(s_{i−1}, h_j)
α_{ij} = exp(e_{ij}) / Σ_{k=1}^{T_{x}} exp(e_{ik})
c_i = Σ_{j=1}^{T_{x}} α_{ij} h_j

parts.desc: h_j: the “annotation” of source word j, the vector the encoder leaves for that word. It contains information about the whole sentence but focuses on the parts around word j.
e_{ij}: the alignment score—how well the decoder state before generating word i, s_{i−1}, matches source annotation h_j.
a: the alignment model, a small feedforward network trained jointly with the whole translation model.
α_{ij}: the attention weight, obtained by applying softmax to the scores for all source words; weights for each step sum to 1.
c_i: the weighted average of all source annotations, giving the context for this step.

formula.note: The paper offers another reading: treat α_{ij} as the probability that the i-th target word is aligned to, or translated from, the j-th source word. Then c_i is the expected annotation over all possible alignments.

plain.title: Every time you write a word, sweep the source sentence with a flashlight
plain.text: Before writing the next target word, the decoder gives each source word a score for how relevant it is. After softmax, those scores become brightness levels that add up to 1. When producing zone, the light lands almost entirely on Area (0.81—the value in the worked table below), and the information from each word is blended by that brightness into a context vector for this step.

blocks.p: The exact form of the alignment model a (Appendix A.1.2) is a(s_{i−1}, h_j) = v_a^{⊤} tanh(W_a s_{i−1} + U_a h_j). It transforms the decoder state and the source annotation separately, adds them, passes the sum through tanh, and projects the result to a single number. Because U_a h_j does not depend on i, it can be precomputed once per source word, saving a large amount of repeated computation. This form was later called **additive attention**, to distinguish it from the dot-product attention used in the Transformer.

fig.title: One worked attention step: when generating “zone,” the model gives 81% of its attention to “Area”
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: the scores and two-dimensional annotation vectors are made up for this walkthrough; the real model's annotations have 2000 dimensions.
fig.note: The raw scores differ by only about 2, but after exponential amplification, Area takes about 80% of the weight. The context c_i therefore lands near Area's annotation while still carrying a little information from the other words. That is “soft” alignment: instead of choosing one word or another, every word gets a share.

callout.title: Why it is called “soft” search
callout.text: Traditional statistical MT first decides which source word corresponds to which target word—a hard, discrete choice that cannot be differentiated directly and has to be estimated as a hidden variable with separate algorithms. Here the weights are continuous and differentiable, so the gradient of the translation error can flow all the way back into the alignment model. As a result, **alignment and translation are learned together under the same objective**, exactly the “jointly learning to align and translate” in the paper's title.

quiz.q: The attention weights α_{ij} are computed with softmax. What does that guarantee?
options: Every source word gets the same weight.
For each target word i, all source-word weights are positive and sum to 1.
Only one source word has a nonzero weight.
The weights do not depend on sentence length.
quiz.why: Softmax turns arbitrary scores into positive numbers that sum to 1, so c_i is a weighted average of the annotations. The model can concentrate attention on one word or spread it over several; it is not forced to choose exactly one. That is what “soft” means.

sections.h: Encoder: a bidirectional RNN so each word's vector sees both sides of the context

blocks.p: Attention requires the encoder to leave a good vector h_j for every source word. A normal RNN reads left to right, so the state at position j only knows the words before it. But translating a word often requires looking ahead: whether English the becomes French le, la, les, or l' depends on the following noun.

So the paper uses a **bidirectional RNN**: one RNN reads left to right, another reads right to left, and the two states at position j are concatenated into h_j. Each word's annotation then summarizes both the preceding and following context. Because RNNs are better at remembering recent inputs, h_j will focus on the area around word j.

parts.desc: →h_j: the state after reading left-to-right up to word j (1000 dimensions), summarizing x_1 through x_j
←h_j: the state after reading right-to-left down to word j (1000 dimensions), summarizing x_j through x_T
Concatenation: the two 1000-dimensional vectors are joined end to end into a 2000-dimensional annotation.

plain.title: One person reads left to right, the other right to left
plain.text: One RNN reads left to right, so at word j it knows what came before; the other reads right to left, so it knows what comes after. Join the two sets of notes at word j, and that word's representation has looked at both sides of the sentence.

blocks.p: The recurrent units are the **gated hidden units** just introduced by Cho et al.—later widely known as the GRU. They have an update gate and a reset gate, similar in spirit to the LSTM: they let gradients flow over long distances instead of vanishing, but with a simpler structure. The paper notes that LSTM units would work here too.

quiz.q: Why use a bidirectional RNN for the encoder instead of an ordinary left-to-right RNN?
options: To make training faster
So each source word's annotation contains both preceding and following context
To make the sentence vector shorter
To handle rare words
quiz.why: Attention uses each position's annotation directly, so ideally each annotation has seen the whole sentence. A unidirectional RNN at position j has only seen the earlier words. A bidirectional RNN is actually more expensive and does not change the vocabulary.

sections.h: Experiments: same data, with and without attention

blocks.p: The paper compares two model types on the WMT'14 English-to-French task: RNNencdec without attention and RNNsearch with attention. Both use the same data and the same training procedure. The WMT'14 English-French parallel corpus has 850 million words, reduced to 348 million using Cho et al.'s data-selection method. The test set consists of 3003 sentences not present in training. Only the 30,000 most frequent words in each language are kept; everything else becomes [UNK].
Each model is trained twice: once with sentences up to 30 words (-30), and once with sentences up to 50 words (-50). Model sizes (Appendix A.2.3):

fig.title: RNNsearch at a glance: 1000 hidden units, 620-dimensional word vectors, 1000-dimensional alignment model
fig.subtitle: From Section 4.2 and Appendix A.2.3 of the paper.
rows: Bidirectional; forward and backward RNNs have 1000 gated hidden units each; annotation h_j is 2000-dimensional.
One layer of 500 maxout units, followed by softmax over 30,000 words.
Minibatches of 80 sentences, stochastic gradient descent plus Adadelta, each model trained for about 5 days.

callout.title: Not directly comparable to Seq2Seq
callout.text: The two papers appeared at almost the same time and used the same filtered WMT'14 data, but their setups differ considerably. Seq2Seq used a 4-layer LSTM, an 80,000-word French vocabulary, an ensemble of 5 models, and reversed source sentences. This paper uses single-layer gated units, a 30,000-word vocabulary, and a single model. So Seq2Seq's 34.81 and this paper's 28.45 cannot be compared directly. Seq2Seq's Table 1 also lists the 28.45 from here.

sections.h: Results: long sentences no longer collapse

fig.title: The attention model leads across the board; on sentences without unknown words, it even beats statistical MT
fig.subtitle: BLEU, from Table 1 of the paper. “Without unknown words” means neither the source sentence nor the reference translation contains a word outside the vocabulary; the model is also forbidden to output [UNK]. Blue columns show those results.
fig.note: The longer-trained model was trained until the validation set stopped improving; it took 252 hours, more than twice as long as the other models. Moses also used an additional 418 million words of monolingual data, which the neural models did not.

blocks.p: Several comparisons stand out. RNNsearch-30, trained only on sentences up to 30 words, scored 21.50—already ahead of RNNencdec-50's 17.82, which was trained on sentences up to 50 words. On sentences without unknown words, the longer-trained RNNsearch-50 reached 36.15, above Moses's 35.63. The paper calls this a significant achievement because Moses also used a separate 418-million-word monolingual corpus.

**Long sentences** are the paper's central evidence. Figure 2 plots test sentences by length: RNNencdec's BLEU drops sharply as length increases; RNNsearch-30 and RNNsearch-50 are far more stable, and **RNNsearch-50 shows no degradation even on sentences above 50 words**.

The paper gives a specific example. The source sentence is: “An admitting privilege is the right of a doctor to admit a patient to a hospital or a medical centre to carry out a diagnosis or a procedure, based on his status as a health care worker at a hospital.” RNNencdec-50 translates correctly up to “a medical centre,” then goes off course, rendering “based on his status as a health care worker at a hospital” as “based on his health condition.” RNNsearch-50 translates the whole sentence completely and accurately.

quiz.q: RNNsearch-30 was trained only on sentences up to 30 words, yet it beat RNNencdec-50, which was trained on sentences up to 50 words. What does this most clearly demonstrate?
options: The data with sentences up to 30 words is higher quality.
The structural improvement from attention matters more than training on longer sentences.
RNNencdec was not trained long enough.
BLEU favors short sentences.
quiz.why: RNNencdec-50 has seen longer sentences and should in theory handle them better, yet it still loses to RNNsearch-30, which has never seen long sentences. The only difference is the architecture: whether attention is present. The paper uses this as further evidence that the fixed-length vector is the bottleneck.

sections.h: Opening the model: attention weights are an alignment map

blocks.p: Attention has an unexpected bonus: **you can see directly what the model is thinking**. Plot each target word's weight α_{ij} over each source word as a grayscale image, and you get a soft-alignment map. Figure 3 of the paper shows four of them.

fig.title: Adjective-noun order is reversed between English and French; attention “jumps” across automatically.
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: simplified from the description in Figure 3(a) of the paper; the values are invented for this article. Rows are generated French words, columns are English source words.
fig.note: English says European Economic Area; French says zone économique européenne, in exactly the opposite order. As the paper describes it, when the model produces zone it skips two words and aligns directly with Area, then works backward one word at a time to complete the phrase.

plain.title: An alignment map reads like a matching game.
plain.text: The x-axis is the English source sentence, the y-axis is the French translation, and a brighter cell means the model was looking more at that English word while writing that French word. Most bright cells run along the diagonal, meaning the translation proceeds roughly in order; where adjective-noun order reverses, the bright cells jump, showing the model learned to reorder words on its own.

blocks.p: What the maps show: English–French alignment is **largely monotonic**, with most weight on the diagonal, but there are also many non-monotonic alignments, such as the adjective-noun order differences above.

**Why soft alignment beats hard alignment**. In Figure 3(d) of the paper, the source phrase the man is translated as l'homme. Any hard alignment would map the to l' and man to homme. But whether the becomes le, la, les, or l' depends on the following word and what letter it starts with. Soft alignment lets the model look at both the and man while generating l', which solves the problem naturally. Soft alignment also handles cases where source and target phrases have different lengths, without hard alignment's awkward need to align words to an empty token ([NULL]).

callout.title: Do attention weights equal the model's reasoning process?
callout.text: Attention maps are intuitive, but they only show where the context vector mainly came from when generating a word. They are not a complete explanation of why the model translated the way it did; the decoder's hidden state and output layer also play a role. Later research has also found that the relationship between attention weights and model decisions is more complicated than it looks. Treat them as a useful window, not a full account.

list: **Compute grows with the product of source and target length**: for every target word, the model scores every source word, so a sentence pair requires T_{x} × T_{y} scoring operations. The paper says most sentences in translation are only 15 to 40 words long, so this is not a problem there, but it may limit other tasks. Three years later, the Transformer had the same quadratic cost, and the cost of attention on long texts remains an active research area.

**Rare words**: the 30,000-word vocabulary penalizes sentences with unknown words heavily (28.45 on all sentences versus 36.15 on sentences without unknown words). The paper's conclusion says better handling of rare words is a future challenge.
**Still a recurrent network**: both encoder and decoder process one word at a time, making training hard to parallelize. Each model took about 5 days to train, and the best model about 10 days.
**English-to-French only**: the paper mentions that language pairs needing long-distance reordering, such as English-to-German, would be harder, but it did not run experiments on them.

blocks.p: **A few small inconsistencies in the paper**: in Section 5.2.1, when describing the alignment map, the same French phrase appears first as zone économique européen and a few lines later as européenne (the latter is the correct feminine form). Section 4.2 says each model was trained for about 5 days, but Appendix Table 2 shows the longer-trained RNNsearch-50 took 252 hours (about 10.5 days); the note to Table 1 already says that version was trained longer.

sections.h: What came next: from “looking back” to attention alone

blocks.p: The paper notes that using a differentiable attention mechanism to focus a network on different parts of its input had already been done by Graves (2013) for handwriting generation, but that attention could only move forward monotonically, which is unsuitable for translation requiring reordering. This paper's attention can jump anywhere in the source sentence, and that is the key to its success in translation.
Following the main thread of this series:

list: **From 2015 on**: attention became a standard part of almost every encoder-decoder model, used in translation, summarization, image captioning, speech recognition, and other tasks.

**2017, the Transformer**: if attention is so useful, why keep the recurrent network? The Transformer uses “self-attention” to let every word in a sentence attend to every other word, removing the RNN entirely and enabling parallel training. It replaced the alignment model here with the simpler scaled dot product, and formally named the roles of s_{i−1} and h_{j} as query, key, and value.
**Today's large language models**: every layer has dozens of attention heads, and each head performs the same three steps from this paper: score, softmax, weighted sum.

blocks.p: Next in the series is GPT-1 (2018): it takes just the Transformer decoder, pretrains it on a large amount of unlabeled text, then fine-tunes it for specific tasks. From here, the main thread shifts from translation to general-purpose language models.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really get it?

quiz.q: If you fixed the context vector c_{i} at every step to the encoder's last forward state, what would the model become?
options: Transformer
An RNN encoder-decoder without attention.
Statistical machine translation.
A bidirectional language model.
quiz.why: The paper's appendix explicitly says that fixing c_{i} to →h_{T_{x}} reduces the model to the RNN encoder-decoder of Cho et al. The entire point of attention is that c_{i} varies with i.

quiz.q: In the alignment model, why can the term U_{a} h_{j} be “precomputed”?
options: Because it is small.
Because it depends only on the source word and not on which target word is being generated.
Because it is a constant.
Because h_{j} is randomly initialized.
quiz.why: U_{a} h_{j} depends only on the source sentence and is identical for every target word, so it only needs to be computed once per source word. At each step, only the decoder-state term W_{a} s_{i−1} has to be recomputed. The paper designed it this way to cut the cost of scoring T_{x} × T_{y} times.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: Why is a fixed-length sentence vector a bottleneck?
How is the context vector c_{i} produced via scoring, softmax, and weighted sum?
How can α_{ij} be interpreted? Why is this called “soft” alignment?
Why does the encoder use a bidirectional RNN? What information does h_{j} contain?
How does the paper show that attention solves the long-sentence problem?
What soft-alignment advantage does the example the man → l'homme illustrate?
What does the computational cost of attention scale with?
How is this attention similar to, and different from, attention in the Transformer?
